question:
Patient note:
A 64-year-old man with a background limited to diet-controlled hyperlipidemia and remote appendectomy was transported by emergency medical services after his spouse found him slumped over the kitchen table complaining of shaking chills and pleuritic discomfort that had begun the previous evening. She reported that he had taken no prescription medications, had not seen a physician in more than a year, and had consumed two glasses of wine with dinner but no illicit substances. During the brief ride he became progressively short-winded; pulse oximetry on ambient air fell to the low 80s, so the crew applied a non-rebreather mask connected to high-flow oxygen, subsequently measured to deliver approximately 65 % inspired oxygen once in the resuscitation bay. The first set of vitals obtained before any intravenous fluids, antipyretics, antibiotics, or analgesics showed a tympanic temperature of 102.8 °F, heart rate 114 beats per minute in sinus rhythm, respiratory rate 21 breaths per minute with mild intercostal effort, and blood pressure 115/64 mm Hg by manual cuff. He opened his eyes only to loud voice, spoke in short phrases that were occasionally disoriented to date, and moved all four limbs to command, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 12 without sedatives or paralytics onboard. Skin was warm and flushed with a fine sweat film; capillary refill was two seconds. No jugular venous distention was noted, and cardiac auscultation revealed a normal S1 and soft S2 without murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Breath sounds were markedly diminished over the right lower posterior lung with coarse inspiratory crackles at the base and egophony just above the diaphragm, while the left lung inflated normally; percussion was dull over the same right basilar region. The abdomen was soft and nontender, bowel sounds present, and no hepatosplenomegaly or flank tenderness was elicited. Extremities showed no edema, and there was no calf asymmetry or tenderness. A radial arterial puncture performed within ten minutes of arrival, still on 65 % oxygen, demonstrated a pH of 7.34, PaCO₂ 37 mm Hg, and when calculated against the contemporaneous alveolar oxygen tension yielded an alveolar-arterial gradient of 184 mm Hg, confirming a substantial defect in oxygen transfer. Laboratory studies drawn from the same stick revealed serum sodium 131 mmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, chloride 99 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 24 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.5 mg/dL—slightly above his wife’s recollection of “normal” values on an old insurance physical but not dramatically elevated. Given an adequate urine output, hemodynamic stability, and only a modest bump in creatinine compared with prior records, clinicians judged that these data did not fulfill criteria for an acute kidney insult. Complete blood count showed a hematocrit of 44 % and white blood cell count 16 500 cells/mm³ with 88 % segmented neutrophils and 6 % bands. Platelet count was 210 000/mm³, and international normalized ratio measured 1.0. A portable chest radiograph obtained before any therapy depicted a dense lobar opacity occupying two-thirds of the right lower lobe with an air bronchogram and small parapneumonic effusion, while the cardiac silhouette and mediastinum appeared normal. Electrocardiogram confirmed sinus tachycardia without ischemic changes. Point-of-care ultrasound demonstrated preserved left ventricular ejection fraction and a collapsible inferior vena cava; there was no pericardial effusion. Urine output since catheter placement in the bay measured 50 mL of clear yellow urine over forty minutes. The patient had no history of chronic lung disease, cirrhosis, heart failure, malignancy, organ transplantation, or systemic corticosteroid use, and he had never required dialysis. He also denied any history of HIV/AIDS, chemotherapy, or other immunodeficiency disorders, and there was no record of advanced organ dysfunction. Vaccinations were reportedly up to date except for skipping the most recent pneumococcal booster. Socially he retired from factory work five years earlier, quit smoking three decades ago after a 15-pack-year exposure, and consumed one to two alcoholic beverages nightly. Blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, and legionella antigen were sent but results were pending at the moment he was transferred to the medical intensive care unit for close hemodynamic monitoring, rapid antimicrobial initiation once cultures were obtained, serial neurologic checks in light of the modestly depressed consciousness, and escalation of respiratory support should gas exchange worsen; no intravenous antibiotics, crystalloids, vasopressors, or antipyretics had been administered before the above findings were documented.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II sums acute physiology points, age points, and chronic health points. Using the available admission measurements:
• Temperature 102.8 °F = 39.3 °C: 3 points. Mean arterial pressure = (115 + 2 × 64)/3 = 81 mm Hg: 0.
• Heart rate 114/min: 2. Respiratory rate 21/min: 0.
• FiO₂ 0.65 requires the alveolar–arterial oxygen gradient rather than PaO₂. Gradient 184 mm Hg (<200): 0.
• Arterial pH 7.34: 0. Sodium 131 mmol/L: 0. Potassium 4.4 mmol/L: 0.
• Creatinine 1.5 mg/dL: 2; no acute renal failure, so do not double. Hematocrit 44%: 0. WBC 16.5 × 10³/mm³: 1.
• Neurologic points = 15 − GCS = 15 − 12 = 3.
Acute physiology subtotal = 3 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 3 = 11. Age 64 (55–64 band) adds 3. No qualifying chronic organ insufficiency or immunocompromise: 0.
Total = 11 + 3 + 0 = 14.
Final answer: 14
